elements.text: Drone Traffic Fingerprinting
What We Can Pick Up, Exploit, and Package

Source research: Christof (2021) DJI Wi-Fi Protocol RE thesis · Behind the Wings (2023) DJI Enhanced Wi-Fi hijacking · OcuSync DroneID analysis (2026) · Detecting Drones via Encrypted Traffic Analysis (2019) · Drone Profiling through Wireless Fingerprinting (2018)
The Problem with the Current Paper
The IJRPR paper's 4-factor model (OUI + packet rate + RSSI variance + SSID) works for basic detection but leaves massive gaps:

rows: Drone with random MAC = 40 points lost
Encrypted traffic indistinguishable from any high-bandwidth client
High false-positive rate in urban environments
Misses newer DJI Air/Mavic on 5.8 GHz
Cannot distinguish drone 50m away from drone 200m away
Cannot differentiate drone type or flight mode

elements.text: Layer 1 — What the ESP32 Picks Up Today (No Changes Needed)
These signals are available from promiscuous 802.11 frame headers alone. No decryption needed. No firmware change required for the basic capture — just smarter processing.

rows: Biometric: small commands vs large video
Who is sending — drone or controller

elements.text: Layer 2 — Traffic Statistics (Encrypted but Classifiable)
These signals survive WPA2 encryption. Multiple academic papers demonstrate 90%+ detection accuracy from these features alone, using as few as 170 packets (820ms of traffic).

rows: No idle gaps >200ms in active sessions

elements.text: Key insight: A smartphone streaming video to YouTube also sends large packets, but it sends both ways (ACKs, control). A drone link is almost entirely one-directional from drone to controller. This asymmetry alone is a powerful classifier.
Layer 3 — Decrypted DUML Protocol (Post-WPA2 Key)
Critical finding from Christof (2021): DJI's Wi-Fi protocol has no application-layer encryption. The DUML payload is plaintext once WPA2 is decrypted. This means:

rows: Classifies every packet as command vs video vs camera
Firm identifier of DJI drone traffic at payload level
Latitude, longitude, height, velocity, pitch/roll/yaw, flight status
Tracks all packets in one flight session
Sequential ordering — detect packet loss or injection

elements.text: What We Can Exploit — Asymmetric Advantages
These are the angles where the defender has inherent advantage over the drone operator:
1. The drone cannot stop transmitting.

A drone in flight requires continuous bidirectional communication. It cannot go silent without initiating return-to-home or landing. This means the detection target is always emitting — no windowing, no intermittent operation.
2. The video stream is a forcing function.

To stream 1080p video at 30fps, the drone must send ~4 Mbps of H.264 data. This requires MTU-sized frames (~1472 bytes) at a sustained rate. No consumer IoT device has this traffic profile. A phone streaming video comes close, but phones have bidirectional ACK traffic — drones don't.
3. The protocol structure is deterministic.

The DJI DUML protocol has fixed delimiters (0x55), known CRC algorithms (CRC-16 Kermit), and fixed field positions. Even without decryption, a 0x55 search at expected offsets within encrypted packets provides a statistical signature for DJI drone traffic.
4. The hardware is cheap.

An ESP32 costs $5. It can already capture all the data needed for Layers 1 and 2 analysis. Adding Layer 3 analysis requires only capturing the WPA2 handshake (same $5 hardware, software addition). This is 1,000× cheaper than commercial C-UAS sensors.
5. The attacker cannot spoof the traffic profile.

To evade traffic-pattern detection, a drone would need to mimic a different device class — changing packet sizes, timing, and directionality. This would require modifying the drone's firmware. Consumer drones don't allow this. Only custom-built FPV drones could attempt it.
What We Can Package — Detection Layers
Proposed five-layer detection model, building on the paper's 4-factor approach:

rows: Known drone vendor prefixes + drone AP names
Drone sends 10-50× more than it receives
0x55 delimiter + CRC-16 Kermit at known offsets

elements.text: Proposed weight redistribution vs the original paper:
Original: OUI(40) + Rate(30) + Var(20) + SSID(10) = 100
Proposed: DirRatio(25) + PktSize(25) + OUI(20) + Timing(20) + Var(5) + SSID(5) = 100
This reduces reliance on MAC OUI (which can be randomized) and elevates traffic-pattern features (which cannot be spoofed without firmware modification).
FPV & Homebrew Drones — Where the ESP32 Goes Blind

The analysis above applies primarily to consumer Wi-Fi drones (DJI in Wi-Fi mode, Parrot, Autel, MAVLink-based drones with Wi-Fi telemetry). FPV and homebrew drones use completely different RF — and the ESP32 cannot see them.
FPV Drones — Invisible to ESP32

rows: RTL-SDR + downconverter, or RF power detector

elements.text: The critical point: An FPV drone emits NO 802.11 frames. The ESP32 sniffer is completely blind to it. The video link on 5.8 GHz is the only reliable passive detection vector — and it requires different hardware.

However: FPV drones still have a video link that must transmit continuously while flying. That 5.8 GHz signal has its own distinctive traits — OFDM preamble signatures for digital links, NTSC sync pulses for analog. These are detectable with a HackRF or even a simple RF power detector tuned to 5.8 GHz.
Homebrew Drones — Paradoxically MORE Detectable When on Wi-Fi
A homebrew drone with a Raspberry Pi or ESP32 companion computer running MAVLink over Wi-Fi is actually easier to identify than a DJI drone:

rows: No heartbeat packet — continuous telemetry stream
Trivial — any Wi-Fi sniffer can decode
Requires WPA2 key capture or statistical analysis

elements.text: Key insight: MAVLink's 1Hz heartbeat is the most reliable drone signature in existence. Every MAVLink drone broadcasts its system ID, component ID, and flight mode every second — in plaintext, over UDP. Any Wi-Fi sniffer within range can identify a MAVLink drone with 100% certainty from a single packet.
Drones Without Remote ID — The Real Detection Challenge
Remote ID (FAA Part 89 / ASTM F3411) broadcasts identification over Wi-Fi or BLE. Drones that don't broadcast Remote ID fall into these categories:

rows: Yes — Remote ID broadcast + Wi-Fi AP
ESP32 + 5.8 GHz Rx for OcuSync path
Not via Wi-Fi — DroneID in SDR signal

elements.text: The hardest detection problem: An FPV drone on ELRS (900 MHz FHSS) with analog video (5.8 GHz NTSC). No Wi-Fi, no BLE, no Remote ID. Detection requires a 5.8 GHz RF energy detector (cheap, but gives only presence, not classification) or an SDR with FHSS tracking capability (expensive, high compute). This is the gap that a $5 ESP32 cannot fill.
Multi-Modal Detection Strategy — Covering All Drone Types

rows: Consumer Wi-Fi drones, MAVLink drones, Remote ID broadcasts
FPV drones, OcuSync-only drones, 5 GHz drones
5.8 GHz video links, requires DSP expertise
Full spectrum coverage in single node

elements.text: Recommended minimum viable stack for broad coverage: One ESP32 (for Wi-Fi drones, MAVLink, Remote ID) + one $10 RTL-SDR dongle with a 5.8 GHz antenna (for FPV video presence detection) + one HackRF (for OcuSync DroneID decode). Total BOM: ~$50-150 per node.
Implementation Path

rows: Add per-MAC packet size histogram + direction ratio to ESP32 firmware. Weight 50% of confidence score.
Add inter-packet timing histogram. Detect 30fps cadence. Weight 20% of score.
Log 4-way handshake from promiscuous frames. Store PMKID for offline decrypt.
Post-process captured PCAPs. Extract telemetry + video from decrypted flows.
TinyML classifier on ESP32 using traffic features. 5-layer model in firmware.
